0.title: Strong in the Lord and in the Strength of His Might
0.essay:
The Bible teaches that there is an unseen world: angels who serve God, and fallen angels who oppose him, led by the devil. Christians make two opposite mistakes about it.

Two mistakes

Some ignore it, living as if the devil were a myth and the spiritual battle unreal. Others become fascinated by it, seeing demons behind every problem and giving the devil far more attention than Scripture does.

The Bible avoids both errors. It takes the devil seriously: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). But it takes Christ far more seriously: “The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

A battle already won

The devil is real, but he is defeated. The Christian’s warfare is not a struggle between equal powers but the outworking of a victory already won. So Paul begins his great passage on the subject not with the enemy but with the Lord: “Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10).

The chapters

The Unseen World — angels and fallen angels; The Enemy and His Tactics; Christ’s Victory; The Armour of God; and Standing Firm, including questions about demonic influence and the occult.

1.title: The Unseen World
1.essay:
Angels appear throughout Scripture: guarding Eden, visiting Abraham, rescuing Lot, announcing Jesus’ birth, strengthening him in Gethsemane, rolling away the stone and freeing Peter from prison. They are created spirits, powerful and holy, who worship God and carry out his will.

Angels serve believers

“Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14). The writer contrasts them with the Son, who sits at God’s right hand. Angels are glorious, but they are servants, and they serve believers.

When an enemy army surrounded the city, Elisha’s servant saw only the soldiers and was terrified. Elisha said, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then he prayed that the young man’s eyes would be opened, “and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17). Faith sees what the eyes cannot: God’s protection is greater than any threat.

When Peter was chained between soldiers awaiting execution, an angel woke him, struck off his chains and led him out past the guards. Peter thought he was dreaming until he found himself in the street (Acts 12:6–11). The church was praying, and God sent his angel.

A missionary family in a dangerous region are frightened after threats against them. They read 2 Kings 6 together and pray. Their fear does not vanish, but they are reminded that they are not alone.

Angels rejoice and wonder

Jesus said “there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10). They watch the work of salvation with wonder; these are “things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:12).

Never worshipped

John, overwhelmed by his visions, fell down to worship the angel who showed them to him. The angel said, “You must not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers the prophets, and with those who keep the words of this book. Worship God” (Revelation 22:9). Paul warned against the worship of angels (Colossians 2:18). Angels point to God, never to themselves. Even the most glorious created being must never be worshipped.

Angels are a different kind of creature from us. People do not become angels when they die. And it is human beings, not angels, whom Christ came to redeem: “For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham” (Hebrews 2:16).

Do we each have a guardian angel? Jesus said of little ones that “their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), and Psalm 91 says God “will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways” (Psalm 91:11). Scripture does not give a detailed doctrine of personal guardian angels, but it assures us that God uses angels to protect his people.

Fallen angels

Not all angels remained faithful. Scripture speaks of “the angels who did not stay within their own position of authority” (Jude 6). These fallen angels, also called demons or evil spirits, follow the devil in opposing God and his people.

A real battle

“For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). Behind much of the world’s evil stand spiritual forces. That changes how we see conflict. Our battle is not against people, even those who oppose us, but against the powers behind evil.

Yet this is not dualism. The devil is not an evil god equal to the good God. He is a fallen creature, entirely under God’s authority, permitted to act only within limits, as the first two chapters of Job show. The powers are creatures, limited and under his sovereign control.

Do you tend to ignore the unseen world, or to be overly fascinated by it?

For reflection

What does Scripture teach about the role of angels? Why must they never be worshipped? How does Ephesians 6:12 change the way you view conflict with other people? Read 2 Kings 6:8–23: how does it encourage you?

2.title: The Enemy and His Tactics
2.essay:
Scripture calls him Satan (the adversary), the devil (the slanderer), the tempter, the accuser, the evil one, the ruler of this world and the father of lies. He is a fallen angel, proud and opposed to God: “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9).

His origin and his limits

Scripture does not give a full account of the devil’s fall. Some find hints in Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28, though those passages speak first of human kings. What is clear is that he was created good and fell through pride (1 Timothy 3:6). And his power is limited. He is not all-knowing, all-powerful or everywhere present. He can do only what God permits (Job 1:12; Luke 22:31).

In Job 1, Satan accused Job of serving God only for what he could get. God allowed him to test Job, but set the limits. Job lost everything, and yet he worshipped. Satan’s accusation was proved false, and God’s sovereignty was proved true.

His aims

The devil seeks to dishonour God, destroy people and hinder the gospel. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” (John 10:10). Jesus told opponents who claimed God as their father, yet wanted to kill him, that they were doing the will of their father the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (John 8:44). Lies and murder are the devil’s native language. Truth and life come from God.

His tactics

Paul wanted believers not to be “outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Corinthians 2:11). Scripture shows several of them.

Deception. He lies about God, about sin and about ourselves. He questioned God’s word in Eden (Genesis 3:1). And “even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), often working through false teaching that looks attractive. His most dangerous work is not obvious evil but attractive falsehood.

Temptation. He tempts us to sin, using our desires, weaknesses and circumstances. He tempted Jesus in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11).

Accusation. He accuses believers before God and in their own consciences, trying to convince them they are beyond forgiveness. He is “the accuser of our brothers” (Revelation 12:10). A believer who has confessed a past sin keeps hearing an inner voice telling her she is too dirty to be forgiven. Her pastor explains that this is the accuser’s voice, and that Christ’s blood has answered every accusation. She learns to answer it with Romans 8:1 and 1 John 1:9.

Division. “Do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Unresolved anger gives him a foothold. He loves to divide churches, marriages and friendships.

Blinding. “The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:4).

Resist, firm in faith

Peter pictures the devil as a roaring lion seeking prey. The response is to be sober-minded and watchful: “Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world” (1 Peter 5:9). Believers are not alone.

And Revelation shows how the battle ends. The great dragon is thrown down; the accuser is cast out. “And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11). The devil is furious, because he knows his time is short.

Not everything is demonic

Scripture distinguishes the world, the flesh and the devil. Not every sin is directly caused by Satan; much comes from our own desires (James 1:14). Not every illness is demonic; most are physical. Wisdom is needed, and it is important not to blame everything on the devil.

Which of his tactics do you most often fall for: deception, temptation, accusation or division?

For reflection

Which names of the devil reveal most about his character? How does he disguise himself as an angel of light today? How can you answer the accuser when he says you are beyond forgiveness? Why does it matter not to blame everything on the devil?

3.title: Christ’s Victory
3.essay:
The most important truth about spiritual warfare is that the decisive battle has already been won.

Promised from the beginning

In Eden God promised that the woman’s offspring would crush the serpent: “he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). The whole Bible looks toward that victory.

Shown in Jesus’ ministry

Jesus cast out demons with a word. They recognised him and trembled. When the Pharisees accused him of casting them out by Satan, he showed how absurd that was — a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand — and said, “But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). He was binding the strong man and plundering his house (Matthew 12:29). His ministry was an invasion of Satan’s territory.

In the region of the Gerasenes, a man possessed by a legion of demons lived among the tombs, beyond anyone’s control. Jesus set him free, and when the townspeople came they found him “sitting there, clothed and in his right mind” (Mark 5:15). Christ’s power restores what the devil destroys.

When the seventy-two returned rejoicing that even the demons submitted to them in his name, Jesus said, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). But he added, “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Our joy is in our salvation, not in power over demons.

Won at the cross

At the cross Jesus defeated the devil. God forgave all our trespasses, “by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross. He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:14–15). The picture is of defeated enemies paraded in a victory procession. And forgiveness and victory belong together: by paying for sin, Christ took away Satan’s power to accuse.

The Son shared our flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Confirmed and completed

Christ rose from the dead and was seated “far above all rule and authority and power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21), with all things under his feet. The devil is defeated but not yet destroyed. At the end, “the devil who had deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur” (Revelation 20:10). His final judgment is certain.

He is like a wounded animal: defeated, and still dangerous. Christ’s victory is complete in principle, and believers live in its power, but the final destruction of evil awaits his return. In the amillennial reading, the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:1–3 describes his restraint during the gospel age, so that he can no longer deceive the nations and stop the gospel spreading. Christ bound the strong man at his first coming.

From victory

“Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). Believers do not fight for victory but from it.

John contrasts the children of God with the children of the devil. Whoever makes a practice of sinning belongs to the devil; those born of God do not keep on sinning, because God’s seed abides in them (1 John 3:8–9). Christ’s victory shows itself in changed lives.

A new Christian who once dabbled in the occult is terrified that the spirits she dealt with will take revenge. Her pastor reads Colossians 2:15 and 1 John 4:4 with her. She learns that she belongs to Christ, who has triumphed over every power, and her fear gives way to peace.

Do you live with a sense of Christ’s victory, or with fear of the enemy?

For reflection

How did Jesus show his power over the devil during his ministry? What happened to the devil’s power at the cross? What does it mean to fight “from victory” rather than “for victory”? Why should our joy be in our salvation rather than in spiritual power?

4.title: The Armour of God
4.essay:
Paul’s most famous passage on spiritual warfare is Ephesians 6:10–18. He wrote it as a prisoner, perhaps chained to a Roman soldier. Notice two things at once: it is God’s armour — we do not make it ourselves — and most of it is the gospel itself.

Be strong in the Lord, and stand

“Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil” (Ephesians 6:10–11). Our strength is not our own; we stand in Christ’s power. The enemy is spiritual, the day is evil, and the goal is to stand firm. Notice how often Paul uses the word “stand”. The Christian’s task is not to conquer new ground but to hold the ground Christ has won.

And notice how the armour is built. The main command is “Stand therefore” (Ephesians 6:14), and the pieces describe what standing looks like. Each piece meets a particular attack.

The belt of truth

A Roman soldier’s belt went on first and held his clothes and sword together. The devil works by lies: about God, about us, about what will make us happy (John 8:44). The truth of God’s word lets us recognise his lies, and an honest life gives him nothing to use. So we test our thoughts against what God has said, and we refuse even small dishonesty.

The breastplate of righteousness

The breastplate protected the heart, where one blow kills. The devil’s deadliest attack is accusation: you are guilty; God cannot accept you. Christ’s righteousness, credited to us, answers it. God accepts us on Christ’s record, not ours. So when we fail, we do not list our good deeds; we confess, and stand on the promise that “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). A holy life matters too, because unconfessed sin gives the devil an opportunity (Ephesians 4:27).

Shoes of the gospel of peace

Soldiers wore studded sandals so that they would not be knocked off their feet. Paul speaks of “the readiness given by the gospel of peace” (Ephesians 6:15). The gospel tells us our war with God is over: “we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). That ground does not move when our feelings do. And it makes us ready to share the good news when someone asks (1 Peter 3:15).

The shield of faith

“In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16). A large shield caught the enemy’s fire arrows before they could start a fire. The devil’s darts are sudden doubts, fears, temptations and accusing thoughts. Faith puts them out by answering them with what God has promised. Name the lie that keeps coming back, and learn the promise that answers it. A thought arriving is not a sin; it becomes ours only if we welcome it.

The helmet of salvation

The helmet protected the head; a blow there could stun a soldier so that he dropped everything. The devil aims at our minds with despair: it is all pointless. The helmet is the sure hope of salvation — Paul elsewhere calls it “for a helmet the hope of salvation” (1 Thessalonians 5:8). God has saved us, is keeping us, and will finish the work. That does not remove grief, but it keeps grief from becoming despair.

The sword of the Spirit

“The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17) is the only weapon for attack in the list. It was a short sword for close fighting. Jesus used it in the wilderness, facing the devil with nothing but the word of God, answering each temptation with “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10) — and the devil left him. We do not need to know the whole Bible to use it, but we need verses we have made our own, so that we can speak God’s word back to the lie when it comes.

Prayer

“Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication” (Ephesians 6:18). Prayer is not one more piece of armour; it is how we put it all on and fight. It runs through everything: at all times, in the Spirit, with perseverance, “for all the saints”. And Paul asks for prayer for himself, “that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains” (Ephesians 6:19–20). Spiritual warfare advances by prayer and proclamation.

God’s own armour

Isaiah saw that there was no justice and no one to intervene. “Then his own arm brought him salvation, and his righteousness upheld him. He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head” (Isaiah 59:16–17). The armour Paul describes is first God’s own, worn by the Messiah, and now handed to his people. None of it is our own achievement.

And it is ordinary. The armour of God is truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, salvation, Scripture and prayer. The devil is resisted not chiefly through special rituals but through ordinary Christian faithfulness. It is also corporate. Paul writes to a church, not just individuals; believers stand together, like soldiers in a line, praying for one another.

A Christian facing intense temptation and discouragement decides to “put on” the armour each morning. She reminds herself of the truth, of Christ’s righteousness credited to her, of the gospel’s peace, of God’s promises and of her secure salvation. She reads Scripture and prays. She still faces battles, but she faces them armed.

Which piece of the armour are you most likely to leave behind?

For reflection

Why does it matter that this is God’s armour, not ours? Which piece do you most need to put on today? How could you grow in using the sword of the Spirit? How does prayer relate to the rest of the armour?

5.title: Standing Firm
5.essay:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:7–8).

Submit, then resist

The order matters: submit to God first, then resist. The devil flees not from our strength but from God’s. And James goes on with a string of commands — cleanse your hands, purify your hearts, grieve over sin, humble yourselves (James 4:8–10). Humility and repentance are weapons against the enemy. God draws near when we draw near.

No foothold

Unconfessed sin, unresolved anger, bitterness and secret habits give the devil an opportunity (Ephesians 4:27). Keeping short accounts with God and with others closes the door. Is there anything in your life, however small, that gives the devil a foothold?

Avoid the occult

As Israel prepared to enter Canaan, God strictly forbade every form of occult practice: “There shall not be found among you anyone who … practices divination or tells fortunes or interprets omens, or a sorcerer or a charmer or a medium or a necromancer or one who inquires of the dead, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD” (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). These were the practices of the nations. God’s people were to listen instead to the prophet he would raise up. Seeking guidance or power from the spirit world is forbidden, and that includes horoscopes, fortune-telling, spiritualism, séances, tarot and contacting the dead.

In Ephesus, some Jewish exorcists tried to use Jesus’ name as a magic formula. The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” and overpowered them (Acts 19:15–16). The name of Jesus is not a charm; its power belongs to those who belong to him. Fear fell on the city, and many believers confessed their practices and burned their books of magic, worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. “So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily” (Acts 19:20).

A young woman has been dabbling in tarot cards and astrology, thinking it harmless. After coming to Christ, she becomes convicted. She throws them away, confesses to God and asks her church to pray with her. She discovers a freedom she did not know she had lost.

Test the spirits

“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). The test is the confession “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (1 John 4:2), and agreement with Scripture.

Do not fear

Believers do not need to live in fear of demons. “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). Christ has triumphed. The devil can tempt, accuse and oppose, but he cannot snatch a believer out of Christ’s hand.

Can Christians be demon-possessed?

Some teach that believers can be inhabited or “demonised” by evil spirits and need deliverance ministry. Others hold that a believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit, cannot be possessed by a demon, though he can be tempted, attacked and influenced.

A true believer cannot be possessed by demons. The believer’s body is “a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19). God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). And he who is in us is greater. The New Testament letters never tell believers to cast demons out of one another. They command them to resist the devil through faith, truth and prayer.

Elaborate rituals, naming spirits and repeated exorcisms of believers have no basis in the letters to the churches. Many problems blamed on demons are physical, psychological, or simply the fruit of sin. Pastoral care should be wise, and medical help sought where needed. Prayer in Jesus’ name, repentance and the word of God are sufficient.

For reflection

What does it mean to “resist the devil”? Are there occult practices in your life or past that you need to renounce? How would you answer someone who says Christians can be demon-possessed? How does 1 John 4:4 give you confidence?
